intro: Five long reads: why shrinking populations and labour-saving AI might cancel out, whether language models can notice their own thoughts, the theorem that closed Einstein's escape route from quantum strangeness, a widow's case against the tidy disposal of the dead, and the real reason St Francis went to see the sultan.

stories.headline: Fewer people, more robots, and no reason to panic
stories.dek: Philipp Humm argues that shrinking populations and labour-saving AI could cancel each other out, leaving rich countries smaller but richer, provided someone decides who owns the machines.
body: Rich countries are doing two contradictory things at once. They spend heavily on baby bonuses, childcare subsidies and visa schemes to make up for a shrinking supply of workers. At the same time they pour money into artificial intelligence and robots whose whole purpose is to need fewer workers. Each policy treats the other's problem as if it did not exist.

Philipp Humm, an artist, author and former technology chief executive based in Milan, thinks the two trends should be read together. In a long essay for Noema he argues that falling populations and falling demand for labour could be complementary rather than catastrophic. The goal, he says, should be to maximise prosperity rather than growth, and the decisive question is not how many jobs survive but who owns what replaces them.

He opens with Aristotle, who imagined in the Politics that self-operating tools would make both masters and slaves unnecessary. Humm thinks the engineering in that passage matters less than its social imagination: what happens to a society whose economy, sense of purpose and welfare state all rest on wage labour, once wage labour stops being the foundation?
## The paradox

The demographic numbers are stark. On United Nations projections cited by Humm, many Western populations could shrink by about 30% by 2100, and Italy's by 40–50%. Family subsidies and immigration have done little to change the trajectory, and the research he draws on suggests immigration's fiscal effect depends heavily on migrants' skills, employment, age on arrival and reason for coming. Meanwhile Britain argues about birth rates, America about immigration, and prominent pronatalists such as Elon Musk and Peter Thiel run companies building systems that reduce the need for human labour.

East Asia, in Humm's telling, is a preview. South Korea has a fertility rate of about 0.75 and spends tens of billions a year on incentives to little effect, yet it has the world's highest robot density, at more than 1,000 industrial robots per 10,000 manufacturing workers. Japan, with one of the most ambitious automation strategies, has over 400, against a world average of roughly 120–150. The countries ageing fastest are also automating fastest.
## A recent invention

Humm's second step is historical. Following Hannah Arendt's The Human Condition, he argues that the labour-centred society is modern. Adam Smith located the wealth of nations in productive labour; around 1800 about 75% of Americans worked in agriculture, against under 2% today; and Henry Ford's 1914 wage rise shows how wages, production and consumer demand came to be bound together. Wages now finance taxes, pensions and welfare. Labour accounts for up to 60% of GDP in OECD countries and private consumption nearly 70%, and Humm cites an OECD-based estimate that each productive hour supports about nine hours of non-working life. If jobs shrink or wages weaken, public finances strain.

Every great technology, he argues, made a scarce input abundant: fossil fuels did it for mechanical energy, globalisation for physical labour. AI may do it for cognition. The old reassurances, Schumpeter's creative destruction and the historical pattern of new jobs replacing old ones, may not hold. He invokes Erik Brynjolfsson's 'Turing Trap', in which AI erodes the cognitive tasks that once let workers climb the value chain, and Daron Acemoglu's point that outcomes depend on whether firms use AI to augment or replace people.

He sees two waves of substitution. The first hits white-collar work: a junior analyst, lawyer, consultant or engineer in London or New York might cost €80–100 an hour, while a language model performs many of the same tasks for a fraction of a cent. The second reaches manual work through humanoid robots from firms such as Tesla and China's Unitree, which he says may eventually cost under $2 an hour against $30–50 for an average American worker. He cites an IMF estimate that nearly 60% of advanced-economy jobs will be affected and almost half face substantial disruption, and concludes that a fall in total employment of roughly 30% is plausible. The exact figure, he stresses, matters less than the direction: labour may stop being the scarcest input.
## The 30/30 equilibrium

Here is the heart of the proposal. If a population falls by about 30% and AI and robotics cut labour demand by a similar amount, the ratio of workers to people stays roughly stable, with no new fiscal strain. Humm is careful to say that this only stabilises things; prosperity depends on capital deepening, as in the Solow-Swan growth model. To hold GDP steady while labour falls 30%, capital productivity would need to rise about 45%, which would lift GDP per head by more than 40%. He thinks the learning curves in semiconductors, computing and robotics make that plausible. By contrast, keeping population constant while capital rises 45% would expand total output by roughly 20%.

He is wary of that second path. Jevons observed that more efficient coal engines increased coal use, and Humm expects cheap AI to raise consumption and environmental costs in the same way. Borrowing Eugene Odum's distinction between pioneer and climax ecosystems, he proposes a 'climax society' that grows prosperity rather than volume. That means dropping two industrial-age assumptions: that economies must expand to repay debt, and that size equals strength. Autonomous drones, he notes, already blunt the military advantage of mass.
## Who inherits the loom?

A stable equilibrium still leaves the distribution question. Under current ownership, automation's gains flow to capital owners, which could undermine demand if workers lose income. Humm considers universal basic income a possible short-term stabiliser but a risky permanent fix: financed by debt it could be inflationary, and taxes on production would largely pass into prices. England's Speenhamland system of 1795, he notes, showed how income support can subsidise low wages and entrench dependence, though he concedes the analogy is imperfect.

His alternative is a 'universal capital dividend'. Governments would take equity or sovereign-wealth stakes in AI infrastructure built on public data, research and infrastructure, and pay the returns directly to citizens. He leans on Marx's notion of a 'general intellect' in the Grundrisse to argue that knowledge is a collective inheritance. The twentieth century solved the demand problem through wages; the intelligence economy, he suggests, might solve it through ownership.
## The devil in paradise

Even if the arithmetic works, two risks remain. One is meaning: Arendt worried about 'worldlessness', and David Graeber's work on pointless jobs suggests that work already supplies purpose badly; a society without much of it must rebuild purpose elsewhere. The other is judgement. Step by step people delegate navigation, search, finance and even legal decisions to algorithms, and their own judgement may atrophy. Humm contrasts a future of 'Homo algorithmus', optimised and dependent, with 'Homo curans', people freed to care.

He hedges throughout. The 30/30 model is a theory of stabilisation, not a guarantee of prosperity. The precise employment figure is uncertain. Outcomes depend on choices about deployment, ownership and purpose, not on technology alone. But his conclusion is hopeful: advanced societies could become fewer without becoming poorer, and live more lightly on the planet while doing so.
stories.counterpoint: The equilibrium assumes the two declines arrive in step, but automation could strip out jobs within a decade while demographic decline unfolds over most of a century, producing mass unemployment first and labour shortages later. It also treats the IMF's exposure figures as job losses, when exposure often means changed tasks. And governments that take equity stakes in AI firms face familiar problems of political meddling and poor returns.
stories.why: Pension systems, health budgets and immigration debates across the rich world assume that a shrinking workforce is a crisis to be fought. If automation can substitute for missing workers, the policy question shifts from how to raise birth rates to how to share the returns of capital, which is a very different argument for voters and finance ministries.
questions: Would you rather your country tried to stabilise its population or tried to grow richer per head as it shrinks?
If AI's returns were paid out as a citizens' dividend, what would you expect to happen to the meaning people find in work?
Which of your own judgements have you already handed to an algorithm, and which would you refuse to?

stories.headline: Can a language model notice its own thoughts?
stories.dek: Researchers have planted 'thoughts' inside AI models to see whether they can report them; the answer, Ben Brubaker reports, is a puzzling and partial yes.
body: Ask someone what they are thinking about and they can usually tell you. That capacity, introspection, is familiar and yet slippery. Philosophers and psychologists still argue over what it is: some tie it to consciousness, others think it is partly an illusion, and almost all agree it is hard to define and harder to test.

Large language models, built from artificial neural networks, now do many things once thought uniquely human. So researchers have begun asking whether they can introspect too. Ben Brubaker, a staff writer at Quanta Magazine, traces the short and lively history of that question, from an experiment at Anthropic that drew wide attention to the sceptical replications that followed. What emerges is neither the claim that models know their own minds nor a clean debunking, but something stranger in between.
## Golden Gate Claude

The central figure is Jack Lindsey, who trained in computational neuroscience, using neural networks to model brains, before leaving academia in 2024 to join Anthropic. His team studied how models work internally and found patterns of neural activity that correspond to specific concepts, from the Golden Gate Bridge to inner conflict. Amplifying such a pattern steers the model's output towards the concept.

In May 2024 Anthropic released a public demonstration, 'Golden Gate Claude', which kept bringing the bridge into unrelated answers. One Reddit post showed it drifting towards the bridge while writing an apple-pie recipe, then apologising and starting over. Lindsey found that moment of apparent self-recognition suggestive, but not proof. The model could simply have read its own output and reacted to it, as anyone might notice a typo.
## Planting a thought

Over the following year he designed a cleaner test. He ran many copies of the same model and injected a concept, such as denim, secrecy or vegetables, into half of them, leaving the rest as controls. Every copy received the same prompt asking whether it detected an injected thought and, if so, what it was about. Crucially, the model had to say whether it noticed anything before it produced any text on the topic, so it could not simply read its own words for clues.

With the most recent and capable version of Claude, models correctly flagged an injection in about 20% of trials, and several also described the concept. In one case, after the team stimulated a pattern associated with capital letters, a model reported an injected thought about something like loudness or shouting. The control copies never reported an injection, which argued against lucky guessing. Lindsey read this as evidence of introspection that is unreliable but real. His 2025 paper was careful: it was limited in scope and made no claim that models have subjective experience. It nonetheless caused a stir online, and other researchers rushed to test it on other models.
## The sceptics' test

Kyle Mahowald, a computational linguist at the University of Texas at Austin, and Harvey Lederman, a philosopher then at the same university, looked for duller explanations. (Lederman has since moved to New York University and Anthropic; Brubaker notes he had no Anthropic connection at the time of the study.) They observed that Lindsey counted a trial a success only if the model both detected the injection and named the concept, and they decided to examine the two abilities separately.

Their worry was that the steering technique was designed to shape output in the first place, so it might make a model talk about a concept whatever the prompt said. Lindsey's injections were gentler than the Golden Gate demo, but they could still nudge. Running the experiment on large open-source models, the pair found that when a model flagged an injection but failed to name it, its guesses were not near misses but simply wrong; 'apple' was a frequent answer. They could also impair naming without affecting detection, suggesting two separate mechanisms. Their conclusion was that the descriptions probably did not reflect introspection.
## The part that will not go away

Detection was another matter. Mahowald and Lederman tried simpler explanations for it and could not make them fit. They describe the ability as 'anomaly detection': a model can sense that something unusual has happened in its own processing without knowing what. Brubaker underlines why this is surprising. Training never involves anyone tampering with a model's internal activity, so there is no obvious reason it should learn to notice such tampering. Lederman called the result mind-bending and said it held up against their controls.

Lindsey's team has since published a follow-up mapping how anomaly detection works inside the model, with similar conclusions. Other researchers have offered 'deflationary' accounts, mostly using smaller models, but none yet explains all of Lindsey's results. Jacob Andreas of MIT says a full deflationary explanation may exist; it simply has not been found. For now, the most defensible reading is the modest one: something in these models registers interference with their own workings, even when they cannot say what the interference was.
## What would count as introspection?

Whether anomaly detection deserves the name is itself disputed. It might be closer to a reflex. Lederman's analogy: if you cut someone and they notice, that is not introspection. But for a model with no body, whose only organ is its network, the line between the physical and the mental blurs.

In a paper this spring, Shauli Ravfogel, Shashwat Singh and Tal Linzen of NYU warned that the word risks meaninglessness, since everything a model does after reading its input involves processing internal states. They proposed tests grounded in leading human theories, especially the idea that introspection involves second-order representations ('I am thinking about apples') rather than first-order ones (the concept of apples). Steve Fleming, a neuroscientist at University College London who studies human introspection, says that distinction turns out to be surprisingly fuzzy in language models, and perhaps in people too.

Some researchers see the work mainly as a sandbox for studying the pressures and mechanisms that might have produced introspection in humans. Brubaker notes that translating results back to psychology is hard. 'Self' and 'other' are unclear concepts for a model, since two copies are identical in a way no two people can be, and Andreas argues identity is central to introspection. Brubaker's conclusion is that machine introspection, if it exists, may look nothing like ours, and that questions once left to philosophers are becoming matters for experiment.
stories.counterpoint: A 20% detection rate on concepts injected by researchers is a long way from a model reliably reporting its ordinary reasoning, which is what safety work would need. The experiments also rely on steering tools whose side effects are poorly understood, so 'anomaly detection' may yet turn out to be a statistical artefact of the intervention rather than a capacity the model has.
stories.why: If models can sometimes notice what is happening inside them, their self-reports could become a useful, if imperfect, window for auditing them; if they cannot, such reports should be treated as storytelling. The experiments also give cognitive scientists a rare chance to test theories of introspection on a system they can open up and manipulate.
questions: Is noticing that something feels off inside you the same as knowing your own mind?
Would you trust an AI's account of its own reasoning more or less after reading about these experiments?
What, for you, would count as convincing evidence that a machine is introspecting?

source.title: New Research Tests Whether AI Models Know Their Own Thoughts
source.author: Ben Brubaker

stories.headline: The theorem that closed Einstein's escape route
stories.dek: A little-known 2012 result, Charlie Wood argues, rules out the commonsense view that quantum mechanics merely describes our ignorance of a definite world.
body: Infants learn object permanence early: a ball hidden behind a cushion is still there, still red, still round. Most adults never question the idea that things have definite properties whether or not anyone is looking. Quantum mechanics has unsettled that assumption for a century. Its mathematics yields only probabilities until a measurement is made, and some of its founders took this to mean there is no single objective reality at all.

In Quanta Magazine, Charlie Wood traces how three moments, Einstein's challenge of 1935, John Bell's theorem of 1964 and a 2012 result known as the PBR theorem, have progressively narrowed the options. His conclusion is that Einstein's version of reality is no longer tenable. Physicists must accept either an objective reality that is surreal or no objective reality at all, unless they can find a new idea of what reality means.
## Einstein's weather forecast

Einstein helped build quantum mechanics and then objected to what it seemed to say. For him reality was the set of objective facts about objects, such as a billiard ball's colour, position and speed, that exist independently of any observer. The theory Heisenberg and Schrödinger developed in the mid-1920s describes possibilities through a wave function. Wood's example is a ball with a 77% chance of being red and a 23% chance of being green. Einstein saw the wave function as something like a weather forecast: useful, but a statement about our knowledge rather than the atmosphere itself.

In 1935 Einstein, Boris Podolsky and Nathan Rosen proposed a thought experiment with two linked particles. Measuring one seemed to reveal properties of the other, implying those properties existed before anyone measured them. The argument rested on two assumptions: reality, that particles have definite states, and locality, that those states can be changed only by nearby influences.

Niels Bohr answered by rejecting the first assumption, insisting there was no quantum world, only an abstract quantum description. His view, later called the Copenhagen interpretation, was rather like saying the forecast is accurate but the atmosphere is indescribable. Many modern physicists find the reply vague, Wood notes, but Bohr's stature and growing experimental success led most to stop asking what the wave function meant. David Schmid, a researcher in quantum foundations, blames Bohr for holding the field back for decades.
## Bell's test

John Bell was more sympathetic to Einstein. In 1952 David Bohm had produced a version of quantum mechanics in which particles have real positions guided by a physical 'pilot wave'. It preserved reality, but at the price of nonlocality: the wave could affect distant particles instantly. Bell then devised, in 1964, a test that applied to any version of quantum theory. In a world that was both real and local, he calculated, measurements on paired particles would agree less often than quantum mechanics predicts. Experiments in the 1980s sided with quantum mechanics. Einstein's two assumptions could not both be true.

That left two broad camps. Bohmian mechanics kept reality and gave up locality; Copenhagen gave up reality. Some physicists wanted a third way, keeping Einstein's idea that the wave function represents knowledge while accepting Bell. In 2004 Robert Spekkens of the Perimeter Institute built a toy model in which particles have definite properties that cannot all be known at once. It reproduced a surprising range of quantum behaviour, including teleportation and the rule that unknown quantum states cannot be copied. Perhaps much quantum weirdness came from reading the wave function too literally. If so, Einstein's forecast analogy might survive after all, with Bell's result accommodated rather than defied.
## The card game

Matthew Pusey, then a graduate student at Imperial College London, read Spekkens's work and tried, with Jonathan Barrett and Terry Rudolph, to build a fully knowledge-based quantum theory. They failed, and then set out to prove that no such theory could exist. The result, published in 2012, is the PBR theorem.

Wood explains it with a card game. A dealer draws from two piles, one of red cards and one of aces, and the player must rule out at least one combination of piles. With ordinary cards, when both cards happen to be red aces the player cannot rule anything out and loses about a quarter of the time. With suitably prepared quantum states, the player can always win. That is possible only if the quantum states are real features of the systems, not mere descriptions of what someone knows about them. The proof rests on two assumptions: that the systems have real states, and that preparing one system does not affect the state of another, a condition Wood notes is distinct from locality.

Experiments have since played the game. A 2012 test supported the quantum winning strategy, and in autumn 2025 a team led by Crispin Barnes of the University of Cambridge extended it to five cards and ran it on an IBM quantum computer, which won as predicted. Barnes's group used the theorem as a benchmark, turning a foundational result into a probe of whether a machine behaves in genuinely quantum ways.
## What is left standing

Many physicists read PBR as proving that the quantum state is real. Wood cautions that this goes too far. The theorem does not exclude the Copenhagen option that nothing is objectively real, in which case the ball's redness depends on its being observed. He recalls Einstein asking Abraham Pais whether the moon exists only when someone looks at it. Pusey frames the choice as biting the bullet or dodging it.

Some have dodged. Jacques Pienaar, once a defender of objective reality, abandoned it after PBR and moved to QBism, which holds that the world may exist but quantum theory describes only relations between systems and agents. Others reject both horns. Lucien Hardy asks whether reality must have a single objective state at each moment and is exploring states that might spread across time. Pusey wonders whether reality is simply 'woolly' and resists strict definition. Schmid says any new account must be so convincing that, once seen, it cannot be unseen.

Wood is clear that these alternatives are early and speculative. What is settled, on his reading, is narrower but striking: under the assumptions Bell and PBR require, the tidy, observer-independent world Einstein wanted is gone. Whatever replaces it will still have to satisfy the intuitions that drew Einstein to the question in the first place.
stories.counterpoint: No-go theorems are only as strong as their assumptions, and PBR's preparation-independence condition is exactly the kind of premise a determined realist can deny, as some retrocausal and superdeterministic models do. Many working physicists would also say the interpretive debate changes no prediction, so declaring Einstein's reality 'killed' overstates what the mathematics forces on anyone.
stories.why: Quantum foundations used to be dismissed as philosophy; now its theorems are used to benchmark quantum computers, which are becoming strategically and commercially important. The debate also bears on a broad question in the philosophy of science: whether our best theories describe the world or only our information about it.
questions: Does it trouble you that our most successful physical theory may not describe an observer-independent world?
Which would you rather give up: an objective reality, or the idea that distant events cannot affect each other?
Can a theory be true if no one agrees on what it is about?

source.title: A Strange Quantum Theorem Has Killed Einstein's Reality
source.author: Charlie Wood

stories.headline: A widow against the tidy disposal of the dead
stories.dek: Writing in Palladium after her husband's sudden death, R. B. argues that modern societies hustle bodies out of sight, strip families of say over them, and lose something civilisational in the process.
body: Most people meet the funeral industry unprepared, in shock, and in a hurry. The choices put to them are few, the paperwork is long, and the default is quiet disappearance. Few stop to ask why the options are so narrow, or who decided that the dead should leave so little trace.

The author of a long essay in Palladium, who signs only as R. B. and is described as a writer and consultant interested in policy and progress studies, had reason to ask. Her husband died of a heart attack in his late thirties, hours after they had woken up together. Her essay is part memoir, part polemic. Its argument is that a society which claims to believe only in what can be measured turns oddly squeamish and spiritual about the one material thing a life leaves behind, and that this embarrassment costs us more than we realise.
## A conversation at the deli

The essay opens some time before his death. A friend's wife had died young of an aggressive cancer, leaving a husband and a young daughter. Over dinner at a Jewish deli, the author's husband told her he had been looking into cryonics and wanted her to consider it seriously. She joked that a clone would be simpler. He replied that a copy would not carry their memories or their story.

When he died, cryonics was not an option: they had never signed up with a provider, and in any case the technology for preserving tissue without ice damage remains unsolved. In a hospital basement in Oakland, the funeral director asked about his final wishes. The choice, she was told, was burial or cremation. Neither matched what she understood him to want, which was to be kept with her.
## Losing custody

Once paramedics took him away, she writes, his body passed in turn to the hospital, the morgue, the coroner's office and the funeral home, and she realised too late that she had surrendered control of it. She accepts that public health and forensic investigation justify oversight. Her complaint is that families retain almost no legal rights over what then happens. Asking to keep a single bone drew a blank; the director said he would look into it.

What galls her most is the inconsistency. Public life, she argues, runs on a strict materialism that credits only what can be measured. Yet the moment a body remains, the same culture abruptly switches to spiritual language, insisting the person has gone and treating what is left as a disposable container to be removed quickly and quietly. The body is said to be meaningless and sacred at once, and in both cases the family is told to let go of it.

Each alternative she explored hit a wall. Cremation at roughly 1,400–1,800°F destroys DNA, leaving remains that are biologically uniform, so identification rests entirely on paperwork. She sets this beside the sequencing of DNA around two million years old and the study of Ötzi, the 5,000-year-old Iceman: science can identify ancient strangers, but a widow could not verify her own husband's ashes after an administrative error. A shared coffin was essentially impossible unless both partners die at once. Exhumation requires protective equipment, negative-pressure tents and disinfectants, several thousand dollars in fees, and legal grounds limited to relocation or forensic examination. Side-by-side burial, so that the wall between coffins might one day decay, recalls Heathcliff bribing the sexton in Wuthering Heights, but modern cemeteries generally require separate vaults.

Donation to science offers no more autonomy. Donated bodies may be sold, dismembered or left to decompose, and she observes that for a few thousand dollars brokers and institutions gain far more control over a corpse than the family ever had.
## What humans used to do

Against this she sets a long human record of keeping the dead. Hunter-gatherers in Asia smoke-dried remains around 10,000 BC. Rosalia Lombardo was embalmed in Palermo in 1920, and the author reckons the chemicals used would cost about $100 today. Excarnation, removing flesh to keep bones in ossuaries, was widespread. Small preservation projects of this kind might cost from several hundred to several thousand dollars, less than a good coffin. She concedes these figures are largely theoretical: licensing, regulation and legal barriers inflate real costs, and applying such methods to human remains is not permitted.

Laws against 'abuse of a corpse' are presented as protection against grotesque display. She thinks they assume everyone wants the same anonymous end, regardless of character, and that the adventurous, irreverent or creative might want something else. Her example is the Sedlec Ossuary at Kutná Hora in the Czech Republic, where the bones of at least 40,000 people are arranged into pyramids and chandeliers. Guides urge visitors to treat it as a sacred site; the national tourism authority sells it with lurid copy. The line between reverence and spectacle, she suggests, has always been blurry.
## From sentience to legacy

The loss changed her philosophy. Before, she was a sentientist: consciousness grounds morality, and the point of life is to prevent suffering. Afterwards she adopted what she calls a more maximalist view. Sentience lasts a few decades; decisions, works and physical form can last centuries. Michelangelo may have spent some days of the Sistine ceiling consumed by neck pain, but measuring his 88 years by his suffering would miss what his life was.

She is frank about grief's irrational pull: she kept medical waste that had touched her husband and treasured a scrap of his burial suit given to her by a friend. She also notes the class politics of funerals. Sellers steered her towards cheaper options; poorer families are nudged towards cardboard coffins and cremation, wealthier ones sold 'tasteful disappearance'. Natural burial grounds certified by the Green Burial Council ban embalming and keep markers tiny or absent. Progress is scant; she cites Oregon's 2023 law letting patients keep amputated body parts as a small step towards bodily rights.
## Why it matters for civilisation

She closes with anthropology. Burial is often taught as the line between culture and nature, though it confers no obvious survival advantage. Her answer is that funerary rites express three things a civilisation needs: care for tangible legacy, respect for others' wishes when no one is watching, and belief in a shared future. Those are the same habits that built pyramids and cathedrals and accumulated scientific knowledge, works their makers often did not live to see finished. Until eternal consciousness or working cryonics arrive, she argues, society should protect the routes to lasting presence we already have.
stories.counterpoint: The restrictions she resents mostly exist for reasons she acknowledges only briefly: disease control, fraud prevention, forensic evidence, and protecting the dead from relatives whose wishes conflict with theirs or each other's. A single grieving spouse's preferences are a shaky basis for loosening rules that also shield the vulnerable, and many religious traditions would see her alternatives as the opposite of respect.
stories.why: Ageing societies are about to bury and cremate far more people, and debates over green burial, body donation and corpse composting are already reaching legislatures. The essay is a reminder that these rules embody a philosophy of the body, and that the materialist default many people accept without thought is itself a choice.
questions: What do you want done with your body, and does anyone who would decide know it?
Is a society's treatment of its dead a fair measure of how much it values the living?
Where would you draw the line between honouring remains and making a spectacle of them?

stories.headline: The friar who went to Egypt to preach
stories.dek: Gabriel Said Reynolds argues that the popular image of St Francis as an interfaith peacemaker before the sultan is a myth, and that the real Francis sought converts and baptism at the risk of his life.
body: Every age remakes its saints. Francis of Assisi has been claimed by environmentalists, pacifists and animal lovers, and the most popular modern story about him concerns his journey in 1219 to the camp of Sultan Malik al-Kamil of Egypt in the middle of the Fifth Crusade. In the familiar telling, the gentle friar crosses enemy lines, embraces the sultan, and shows a better way than the Crusaders' swords.

Gabriel Said Reynolds, who teaches theology and Islamic studies at the University of Notre Dame, thinks that story owes more to the present than to the sources. In an essay in the November issue of First Things, he argues that Pope Francis's 2020 encyclical Fratelli Tutti, which opens with this episode, presents a mythical Francis. The historical Francis, Reynolds contends, went to Egypt to preach Christ and call Muslims to baptism, and was ready to die for it.
## The encyclical and the imam

Fratelli Tutti presents Francis's visit as an openness that transcended differences of origin, nationality, colour and religion, and as evidence of the breadth of his love. The encyclical draws explicitly on Pope Francis's meeting with Ahmad Al-Tayyeb, grand imam of Al-Azhar, Egypt's leading Sunni institution, and on their joint Document on Human Fraternity for World Peace and Living Together, signed in Abu Dhabi on 4 February 2019. That meeting was timed for the 800th anniversary of the encounter at Damietta. The two leaders embraced on stage, and an icon by the Franciscan Robert Lentz shows saint and sultan side by side, both haloed and both labelled 'saint'. The implied parallel was plain: God had raised up men of peace in both centuries.

The saint was central to Pope Francis's self-understanding. He was the first pope to take the name, he titled two encyclicals after Francis's Italian sayings, and he signed Fratelli Tutti in Assisi on 3 October 2020, the vigil of the saint's feast. The reception was warm. Christine Allen of the Catholic aid agency CAFOD praised its universal message, and Massimo Faggioli, writing in Commonweal, used the signing date to draw a contrast with Joseph Ratzinger: on 3 October 2000 a planned Jewish-Christian dialogue had been cancelled in the wake of Dominus Iesus, the declaration issued by Ratzinger's doctrinal office.

Reynolds recounts the background. In 2010, after a New Year's bombing of a church in Alexandria killed more than twenty people, Benedict XVI raised the persecution of Egypt's Christians. Al-Tayyeb suspended Al-Azhar's dialogue with the Vatican over this 'interference', claiming that Christians persecute Muslims more. Under Pope Francis dialogue resumed; the two men met nine times between 2016 and 2022.
## A questionable partner

Reynolds grants that the Holy See's diplomatic calculations are complicated. But he argues Al-Tayyeb is a poor co-author for a document on fraternity. The grand imam has worked closely with the Sisi government, whose record Amnesty International has called a decade of shame, marked by arbitrary detention and unfair trials. Reynolds says Al-Tayyeb has backed the traditional rule that converts from Islam must return or face execution, supported blasphemy prosecutions, and opposed religious freedom for Baha'is. With Al-Azhar's backing the state refuses to change converts' identity cards to read Christian; in July 2025 one such convert, Saeid Mansour Abdulraziq, was arrested on terrorism and contempt-of-Islam charges, apparently without objection from Al-Tayyeb. Reynolds quotes Rashied Omar, a Muslim imam who teaches at Notre Dame, on how Middle Eastern religious leaders have become state appointees who legitimise state power.
## What the Rule actually says

The heart of the essay is a textual argument. Fratelli Tutti cites Francis's Earlier Rule on how friars should live among 'Saracens and other nonbelievers', quoting its counsel to avoid arguments and disputes and to be subject to every human creature for God's sake. Reynolds calls the quotation selective. Chapter 16 of the Rule offers two ways of living among non-Christians. The first is that quiet witness: no disputes, humble submission, open acknowledgement of being Christian. The second, when it pleases the Lord, is to proclaim the word of God so that hearers believe in the Trinity and are baptised, because no one can enter the kingdom of God without being reborn of water and the Spirit, an allusion to John 3:5.

From this Reynolds draws a doctrinal conclusion. Francis was not opposed to the open evangelisation of Muslims, and he believed they could be saved only through baptism. A Francis who sought merely to coexist, or who regarded the sultan's faith as an equally valid path, is not the author of the Rule.
## The earliest witness

Reynolds then turns to the historical sources, guided by John Tolan's study Saint Francis and the Sultan. The earliest is a letter by Jacques de Vitry celebrating the fall of Damietta in November 1219. Two versions mention Francis; a third, sent to the pope, omits him. The letter says Francis crossed into the enemy camp, preached to the Saracens for several days with little success, and that the sultan asked him to pray that God would show him the religion most pleasing to him.

Around 1224 Jacques's Historia Occidentalis added detail: Francis was captured, brought before the sultan, preached the faith for days, and was released because the sultan feared his soldiers might convert, a fear Reynolds notes was grave since apostasy meant death for a Muslim soldier. Reynolds treats some of this as embellishment. But in none of these accounts is Francis a peacemaker. He is a preacher seeking conversions. Reynolds adds that nothing in Francis's writings condemns the Crusades, and that the line usually attributed to him about preaching the gospel and using words only if necessary does not appear in this context.
## Fortitude, not fraternity

For Reynolds, Francis's courage lay in preaching Christ to Muslims under threat of death. He recalls the five friars Francis sent to Morocco, Berard, Peter, Otho, Accursius and Adjutus, who were beheaded in 1220. Fratelli Tutti says Francis did not wage a war of words but simply spread God's love; Jacques's account is of earnest, largely fruitless preaching.

His conclusion is pointed. The encyclical's vision of a peaceful, diverse global society was not St Francis's. It also leaves Catholic men, Reynolds argues, with only two models: the bigoted Crusader or the meek peacemaker. The real Francis offers a third, a man who risked his life to preach the gospel. Few will retrace his journey, but all can learn his fortitude. There is no need, Reynolds ends, to invent a new Francis, because the real one was a saint.
stories.counterpoint: Reynolds's own sources show Francis choosing to preach rather than fight, entering the camp unarmed while a crusading army besieged Damietta, and the Rule's first option of quiet, non-disputing witness is as authentically his as the second. A reading in which Francis was both an evangelist and, by his manner, a rebuke to crusading violence may be truer than either the encyclical's or Reynolds's.
stories.why: How the church remembers its saints shapes how it understands mission. For preachers and teachers, the episode is a case study in letting primary sources correct a cherished illustration, and in holding together gentleness of manner with the conviction, grounded in texts like John 3:5, that the gospel calls all people to new birth.
questions: Which favourite sermon illustration of yours might not survive a look at the original sources?
Can interfaith friendship and a clear call to conversion be held together, and how did Francis attempt it?
Where does your own witness need more of Francis's fortitude, and where more of his gentleness?
